OFFICIAL RESULT PUBLISHED SEPTEMBER 22, 2026: $889M — RECONCILED AGAINST THE ~$489M DOCUMENTED FLOOR
Visit Seattle published the official post-event result on September 22, 2026: $889M total impact, $109M state and local tax, ~20,000 jobs — above the revised $845.6M forecast and below the original $929M projection. The analysis was prepared for Visit Seattle by Tourism Economics; its full report, multiplier and displacement treatment have not been released publicly. Independently, this analysis models a documented floor of ~$489M using the 6-Pillar Framework with 5-method triangulation and displacement adjustment. This floor is 42% below the revised $845.6M forecast; the assumption bridge reconciles it to the official $889M. Calculated direct spending: ~$391M. Calculated tax estimate: ~$15.5M (4-method from actual KC/Seattle receipts). NY/NJ post-event: $3.5B (+6% above forecast).

The tournament had a radius. Inside about a mile of Lumen Field it delivered everything promised; beyond it, the effect thinned quickly, and some neighbourhoods went backwards. Every page of this dashboard is one angle on that fact. Follow the five chapters below, or jump to any page from the navigation.

THE OFFICIAL FIGURE IS NOW PUBLISHED — $889M

Visit Seattle released its post-event economic impact report on September 22, 2026, reporting $889 million in total economic impact for Seattle and King County, $109 million in state and local tax revenue, and approximately 20,000 jobs supported. That result lands below the original $929M December 2024 projection and above the $846M forecast revised in March 2026.

The gap between that headline and the $489M modeled independently here is not a data dispute. It resolves into three modelling choices: the 12% displacement adjustment, the 1.42× RIMS II multiplier versus the 1.84× implied by Tourism Economics’ New York/New Jersey study, and assumed spending per visitor. Applying all three alternatives to the same underlying evidence produces roughly $850M — within 5% of the published $889M. The bridge was built before the report was issued and it held. See Benchmarks & Reconciliation for the step-by-step derivation.

The ADR surge (+30.5%) was real but didn't translate to proportional economic impact because occupancy was flat.

Evidence Classification System

Class A — Official measured data from government/agency sources (FIFA, Sound Transit, ESD, SPU)

Class B — Provider sample data from commercial platforms (CoStar/STR, Placer.ai, Square, Toast, Datafy, AirDNA, HVS)

Class C — Appropriation/authorization data from legislative sources (WA Session Law, Seattle ordinances, King County budget)

Class D — Published forecast/model, not realized outcome (Tourism Economics $929M / $845.6M projections)

Class E — Not publicly available; requires direct data-owner access (DOR tax receipts, FIFA ticket origin, granular ZIP spending)

PUBLICATION RULE
Forecasts are "verified" only in the sense that a named source really published the forecast. They are not verified realized outcomes. They must not appear in a headline that says "FIFA generated $X" until the post-event model is reconciled to actual visitor, spend, tax, labor and public-cost data.

ONE PATTERN IN EVERY MARKET THAT HAS REPORTED

Houston’s convention bureau: occupancy down 1%, hotel revenue up 20% on rate. Boston: occupancy matched 2025 while rates rose 20.7%. Seattle: occupancy down, rates up. A Seattle hotel advisory firm summed up the local market in six words — “a rate event, not an occupancy event.” Seattle’s distinction is that it had the furthest to fall: Tourism Economics classed it before the tournament as a high-season market with typical June occupancy above 80%, so there were few empty rooms for the event to fill and many regular visitors to crowd out.

Same modeller, different ratios. Tourism Economics prepared both the Seattle and NY/NJ results. Tax runs at a similar share of impact in both — 12.3% in Seattle, 11.8% in NY/NJ. Jobs do not: Seattle reports ~22.5 jobs per $1M of impact against ~7.8 in NY/NJ. That gap is one of the first questions to put to the Seattle workpapers when they are released.

Per match, NY/NJ generated ~$438M against Seattle’s ~$148M; per stadium attendee, ~$5,400 against ~$2,200 — consistent with NY/NJ hosting the final and drawing the larger international contingent. CMRE Partners Houston First Tournament: 6,810,966 attendance

Benchmarks & Reconciliation
The official $889M Visit Seattle result, independent post-event measurements, host-city benchmarks, and an auditable bridge from the $489M documented floor to the official figure
Visit Seattle published its post-event economic impact report on September 22, 2026: $889 million total impact, $109 million in state and local tax revenue, approximately 20,000 jobs. The assumption bridge below was constructed before that release and arrived at roughly $850M — within about 4.4% of the published figure. The $489M modeled here and the $889M official result are not in conflict on the underlying evidence; they differ on three named, disclosed modelling choices: the displacement adjustment, the output multiplier, and per-visitor spending. None of the three is a data error on either side.

HOW THE OFFICIAL RESULT COMPARES TO ITS OWN FORECASTS
The published $889M is 4.3% below the original $929M projection and 5.1% above the $845.6M revised forecast. Visit Seattle attributes exceeding the revised figure to three specific factors: more international fans attending matches than the revision assumed, more overnight visitors attending watch parties, and the effect of a second United States men’s national team match in Seattle. The revision itself had been driven by weaker inbound international travel and slow hotel booking pace.
THE OFFICIAL REPORT ALSO DOCUMENTS MIXED HOSPITALITY RESULTS
The same report does not describe a uniform boom. Visit Seattle reports that hotel occupancy declined year over year and that higher room rates — not higher volume — drove the increase in overall hotel revenue. It records that some businesses had record weeks while others saw a year-over-year dip in sales, and that cruise passengers and convention attendees were displaced by the tournament. This is consistent with every independent measurement in this dashboard: rate-driven lodging revenue, Seattle posting the largest occupancy decline of the eleven host markets in the HVS study at −6.3 points, and sales declines of up to 22% in the Chinatown-International District.

A MOSTLY LOCAL AND DOMESTIC CROWD

Coverage of the release described the crowd as more local and domestic than international, and Visit Seattle’s activation lead explained why — Seattle drew no team with a travelling mass fanbase: “We didn’t get the Argentinas of this world. We didn’t get the Brazils of this world.” The airport confirms it — June–July passengers were flat to the hundredth of a percent, with a slight international gain offset by a slight domestic dip.

Two implications follow. First, 55% of the ~1.3 million visitors were from Seattle itself, and part of the 45% came from elsewhere in King County — inside the study area. Spending by residents is largely reallocated local money rather than new money, which is exactly what a displacement adjustment captures. Second, the three reasons Visit Seattle gives for beating its revised forecast — more international fans than feared, more overnight visitors at watch parties, and a second USMNT match — all concern the margin above a lowered bar, not a flood of new visitors.

WHY BOTH NUMBERS BELONG IN EVERY BRIEFING
$889M is the official result and should be cited as such. $489M is the receipts-and-measurement floor built only from figures with a published source, using a conservative multiplier and an explicit displacement deduction. The two bracket the honest range. The value of holding both is that the difference is fully accounted for: it is three disclosed assumptions, not a disagreement about what happened. When the methodology behind $889M is released, the bridge in the next section can be reconciled against it directly.
1 · Methodology Bridge — $489M to the Official $889M
StepAssumption changedEffectRunning totalBasis
Base6-Pillar 5-method triangulation: $391.5M direct × 1.42 × 0.88—$489MIndependent modeled estimate
1Remove the 12% displacement adjustment+$66.7M$555.9MTE’s NY/NJ study discloses no displacement haircut
2Raise the multiplier from 1.42× to 1.84×+$164.5M$720.4M1.84× is TE’s implied NY/NJ multiplier: $3.5B total ÷ $1.9B direct
3Raise per-visitor spend from $994 to ~$1,173 (+18%)+$129.6M~$850MTE’s NY/NJ direct visitor spend implies ~$2,714 per non-local visitor
—Official Visit Seattle published result, Sep 22, 2026—$889MBridge lands within 4.4% of the official figure
HOW TO READ THE BRIDGE
Each step is a single, named, defensible modelling choice — not a correction. Removing displacement and adopting a 1.84× multiplier alone moves $489M to $720M. A further 18% increase in assumed per-visitor spending reaches roughly $850M. The reverse also holds: applying this analysis’s assumptions to NY/NJ would reduce that region’s $3.5B materially. The 1.84× figure is derived from Tourism Economics’ disclosed NY/NJ totals ($1.9B direct, $693M indirect, $916M induced, $3.5B total); TE does not publish it as a multiplier. This analysis uses the 1.42× RIMS II midpoint for Washington accommodation and food services, and a 12% displacement adjustment supported by locally measured business results.

WHY NEW YORK IS NOT A FAIR YARDSTICK FOR SEATTLE
NY/NJ hosted the Final and eight matches including knockout rounds; Seattle hosted six, none past the Round of 32. HVS attributes $339.2M of the $680M national incremental rooms revenue to New York alone — roughly half the US total from a single market. New York also enters June from a lower seasonal occupancy base, leaving room for the tournament to fill, while Seattle’s June baseline already runs above 80%. The divergence between the two regions is a function of match inventory, stage progression, room inventory and baseline seasonality.

SEATTLE IS THE WEAKEST HOTEL OUTCOME OF THE ELEVEN US HOST MARKETS
HVS’s counterfactual analysis names incremental rooms revenue for the five largest markets and groups the remaining six — Seattle among them — as each generating under $25M, in a band running from $23.7M down to $8.2M. The five named markets account for $580.7M of the $680M national total, leaving roughly $99.3M spread across all six remaining cities. Seattle simultaneously recorded the largest occupancy decline of any US host city at −6.3 percentage points, with an ADR gain of $26.56 and a RevPAR gain of $26.60, or +15.7%. The tournament raised Seattle’s room rates while reducing the number of rooms sold.

A CRITICAL DISTINCTION FOR IMPACT CLAIMS
Overseas arrivals from World Cup participating countries fell 1.1% year over year in June and July. They outperformed the −8.9% recorded for non-participating countries, but the tournament did not produce absolute growth in overseas arrivals — it produced relative outperformance against a declining national baseline. Impact figures built on an assumption of absolute international visitor growth are not supported by the arrivals data.

THE RATE-VERSUS-VOLUME PATTERN, CONFIRMED THREE WAYS
Seattle ADR ran roughly 30% above the prior year during the peak match week while occupancy during match weeks ran several points below baseline, producing only a modest net RevPAR gain. Citywide June ADR finished about 10% higher year over year. This is the same pattern HVS records as a $26.56 ADR gain against a 6.3-point occupancy loss, and the same pattern Tourism Economics describes nationally as revenue growth “driven largely by higher room rates.” Rate-driven revenue accrues to hotel operators; it does not represent additional visitors, additional nights, or proportionally broader spending across the local economy.

Link ridership YTD: 23.253M actual vs 20.645M budget — 113% of budget; the June monthly figure surpassed budget by 20%

Ridership variance contributed +$4.3M of fare revenue above budget: Link +$3.8M, ST Express +$0.3M, Sounder +$0.2M, T Line $0.0M

Average fare per boarding contributed −$0.3M below budget — a fare-compliance signal consistent with the 58–74% paid share

By mode: Link +$4.2M, Sounder +$0.2M, ST Express +$0.2M above budget

YTD revenues and other financing sources of $1,455M were $63M or 5% above budget, driven by sales tax, federal grants and fare revenue

Operationally: World Cup temporary staffing went unutilized; charter bus services ran over budget; T Line overtime rose on World Cup operations; DSTT Modernization underspent on track-access limits; Facility Property underspent under a World Cup construction moratorium; Kent Garage repairs were delayed

King County ECONPULSE, Q2 2026 Class A

Seattle recreation price index +9.8% year over year in June 2026. The County states World Cup activity in the latter part of June likely influenced this growth — the clearest official price-effect evidence available.

King County total employment: −4,900 jobs (−0.3%), Q2 2026 vs Q2 2025

Leisure and hospitality: +1,400 jobs (+1.0%). The County attributes World Cup gains to retail, food service and accommodation, and recreation.

2026 sales tax revenue projected at $1.52B, +14.8%, with taxable sales up more than 8% for the year; the July forecast attributes 7.3% growth to the expanded tax base and World Cup activity, footnoted “Includes World Cup impacts in 2026”

2026 property tax revenue projected at $1.74B; assessed value +5.4%; new construction +3.4%

The report expects additional hotel, lodging and rental car tax revenue from the June and July matches but discloses no quantified World Cup–specific revenue figure. Its county-level quarterly employment measure and state monthly sector counts are different bases and should not be netted against each other.

Counting and Payment Basis Methodology

Passenger counts come from lasers inside railcars, not ORCA taps or fare revenue, which is why they exceed payment records. Not all railcars carry counters, and further data downloads have revised figures upward.

June 2026: 5.4M Link boardings, the highest month on record, averaging 180,000 per day

Jun 19: 172,296 payments recorded across ORCA, credit/debit, Transit GO and vending machines, plus 46,083 paper tickets. Treating every paper ticket as a round trip or day pass gives 218,379 paid rides, or nearly 74% of the 297,000 riders; Sound Transit brackets the paid share at 58–74%.

2025 comparison: 61% of riders paid. Early 2026 performance was similar.

Riders aged 18 and under ride free and are estimated at 6–9% of ridership, reimbursed through the state transportation budget. Sound Transit had not calculated June fare revenue at the time of reporting and expected the calculation to take months.

10 · Displacement and Spatial Concentration
Chinatown–International District Negative

At a July 1, 2026 media conference, CID businesses reported sales declines of as much as 22% over the prior two months against the same period a year earlier — despite the district sitting roughly a 10-minute walk from the stadium.

This is the strongest locally measured support for a non-zero displacement adjustment. The 12% displacement factor applied in this analysis sits well inside what this observation would permit.

Pioneer Square and Adjacent Corridors Positive

Pioneer Square business organisations reported on June 25, 2026 that several establishments recorded their strongest sales performance in recent years. Moonshot Brewing reported +30% across the World Cup months.

Other stadium-adjacent businesses reported declining sales over the same window. The combined evidence shows sharp spatial concentration within a few blocks rather than a uniform citywide lift — precisely the pattern a displacement adjustment exists to capture.

Community Business Connector Grants Class B

$250,000 distributed in Game Ready Activation Grants

23 organisations supported · 72 community activations

17,131+ King County community members engaged · 248 local businesses showcased

65% of grantees planned to host similar events during the tournament itself.

Fiscal Context from Third Parties Class C/D

Local governments and agencies in Washington expect to spend $24M more to host the tournament than they will receive in boosted tax revenue — an independent, statewide-scope result in the same direction as this analysis’s Seattle-scope −$16.5M net fiscal return. The two cover different geographies and are not substitutes.

US host cities have been characterised as “a wash,” unlikely to recoup nine-figure investments.

Host cities receive no share of ticket, concession, merchandise or parking revenue — a structural reason municipal revenue capture lags attendance.

Academic work argues mega-event impact studies systematically overstate net benefits by omitting substitution and displacement.

PUTTING $489M AND $15.5M IN PROPORTION
The $489M modeled impact equals roughly 5.6% of one year of King County visitor spending. The $15.5M calculated tax estimate equals roughly 1.8% of the $840M in state and local taxes the hospitality industry generates annually. The region entered 2026 from a base that was contracting slightly in both visitors and spending, not expanding — which matters for any counterfactual about what would have happened without the tournament.

PUBLICATION STATUS OF THE RECONCILIATION DOCUMENTS

The $889M analysis was prepared for Visit Seattle by Tourism Economics (Axios), the same firm that produced the New York/New Jersey post-event study. The Seattle report document itself has not been released publicly — only its headline totals. That matters for the bridge below: because both the $889M and the NY/NJ $3.5B come from the same modeller, deriving the multiplier and per-visitor benchmarks from TE’s disclosed NY/NJ internals is a like-for-like comparison, not a cross-model one.

Visit Seattle’s post-event report was released September 22, 2026. Visit Seattle’s own release, and coverage by the Seattle Times, Axios, KNKX/OPB, KING 5, KOMO and MyNorthwest, report the headline totals — $889M impact, $109M state and local tax, approximately 20,000 jobs, around 1.3 million visitors to matches and watch parties. The underlying report document, its methodology, multiplier, displacement treatment and per-visitor spending assumptions have not been published, so the $889M figure cannot yet be reconciled line-by-line or independently replicated.

No SeattleFWC26 Local Organizing Committee After Action Report has been published.

Washington lodging tax actuals cannot yet be verified by any party. The state legislature’s lodging tax reporting system does not open until January 1, 2027 for 2026 revenue and expenditure data. This is a calendar-driven constraint, not a limitation of this analysis.

Consequently the $889M headline is reported but not yet auditable: the modeller is known, but its workpapers are not public. Every figure presented in this analysis is traceable to a published source, and the bridge in Section 1 shows exactly which assumptions move $489M to that range. The appropriate posture for decision-makers is to cite $889M as the official Visit Seattle result while requesting the underlying methodology, and to treat the $489M as the conservative, fully-documented floor.

THE CENTRAL FINDING: ACTIVATION MODEL DETERMINED THE OUTCOME

The host-venue model worked. In Maple Valley–Black Diamond the chamber distributed funds to individual businesses that hosted viewing in their own establishments. Those businesses already had the space, screens, staff and licences, so incremental cost was low — $1,925 across four businesses — and every dollar of attendance converted into sales at their own margins. Result: +$7,701, a fourfold return on what businesses spent, with zero unprofitable participants. White Center’s district-wide art walk model performed similarly on a small base, at +$2,060 on $640 spent.

The central-festival vendor model did not. Federal Way concentrated activity at a single venue with vendor booths. Participating businesses bore booth fees, inventory, transport, permits and staffing before earning anything — $22,595 spent, 82% of all business spending across the entire program, to generate $11,577. Twelve of thirteen Federal Way businesses did not make a profit. This is where the Chamber’s next dollar has the most to gain from a design change.

What the Investment Did and Did Not Produce
Delivered Measured

Community connection — the single most-cited benefit, named by 17 of 28 businesses, ahead of every commercial outcome

Event-readiness capacity — 12 of 28 gained confidence participating in future activations; 8 gained experience preparing for larger events

Labor — 99 additional workers and 312 volunteer hours; 11 businesses increased hours for existing employees, 3 added temporary staff, 9 drew on volunteer or family support

Reach — 222 small businesses touched beyond the organizing bodies; organizers reported 7 of 8 seeing new customers and visibility gains for participants

Spillover — 4 of 8 organizers confirmed non-participating neighbours benefited from foot traffic; the remaining 4 were unsure, none said no

Media — 5 of 8 activations earned press or public recognition, including neighbourhood blog coverage of the White Center art walk

Did Not Deliver Measured

Profit — 17 of 28 businesses did not profit; only 7 did

New customers — 18 of 28 reported none or very few; just 1 reported most

Brand awareness — 17 of 28 saw no noticeable change in awareness of their business

World Cup pull — 17 of 28 said the World Cup theme had no noticeable impact on attracting customers. The theme was not, by itself, the draw.

Attendance — 18 of 28 businesses named low attendance or customer traffic as their leading challenge, by a wide margin over every other option

Follow-on business — 15 reported no follow-up sales, bookings, leads or referrals; 9 reported some, 4 expect some later

WHY PARTICIPANTS STILL WANT TO COME BACK
The gap between the financial result and the 20 of 28 businesses and 7 of 8 organizers who want to do this again is the most important thing in these surveys. Businesses did not enter primarily for profit: their top three motivations were promoting the business to the community (22), reaching new customers (21), and participating in a cultural celebration (18), with increasing revenue fourth at 16. The fund bought civic participation, district activation and event-readiness — not near-term sales. Reporting it that way is both accurate and stronger than a revenue claim the data does not support. 18 of 28 want information about future readiness resources and funding, and 14 agreed to an on-record interview or business spotlight.

READING THE ORGANIZER TOTALS WITH CARE
Attendance sums 7 of 8 activations; the Maple Valley–Black Diamond chamber stated that because its role was administering and distributing grant funds rather than hosting, it could not provide attendance or participation figures for the individual watch parties. Vendor sales were reported by only 4 of 8 organizers, so the $26,500 is a floor, not a program total. The 222 businesses reached is a sum of organizer self-reports and may double-count businesses that participated in more than one activation — notably the two White Center events, which together report 86. Attendance met or exceeded expectations for 6 of 8 organizers; one was much lower than expected.

Lead Time Was the Dominant Complaint Qualitative

Short notice appears in open-text answers across both surveys more than any other theme. Organizers described making adjustments to established events on compressed timelines; businesses described being unable to market.

One Skyway organizer reported both participating businesses “struggled with the last minuteness” and had smaller turnouts as a result.

A Federal Way business stated it would have advertised heavily, including in local print, with earlier notice. Another concluded that in-person flyers and promotional cards would have outperformed the digital advertising it ran.

Specific Design Complaints Qualitative

Booth placement. Multiple Federal Way vendors reported being positioned behind the stage, out of customer sightlines. One stated plainly that knowing placement in advance would play a major role in success.

Uneven voucher access. One vendor reported that some businesses at the same location received attendee vouchers redeemable at their booths while others did not, and asked to be included next time.

Cuisine overlap and logistics. A food vendor asked for no duplicate cuisine categories, overnight parking for perishable stock, and realistic attendance projections.

Fee structure. One business proposed a percentage-of-sales model instead of a flat fee so that cost scales with actual traffic.

Recommendations for the Next Activation Cycle
#RecommendationEvidence base
1Default to the host-venue model. Fund existing licensed venues to host in their own space rather than assembling vendors at a central site.Maple Valley–Black Diamond returned +400% on business spend with 0 of 4 unprofitable; Federal Way returned −49% with 12 of 13 unprofitable
2Eliminate or reimburse up-front booth and participation fees. Where a central format is used, convert flat fees to a percentage of sales or cover them from the grant.11 of 28 businesses paid venue or booth fees; fixed pre-sale cost is the direct mechanism of the Federal Way deficit; a participant independently proposed the percentage model
3Set a minimum 8–12 week notification window. Announce awards early enough for businesses to market and order stock.Short lead time is the most frequent open-text complaint across both surveys and is tied directly to reported low turnout
4Fund district-level marketing centrally rather than per business.14 of 28 businesses each paid separately for marketing; 20 businesses and 7 organizers name promotion support as a need; awareness gains were not achieved in 17 of 28 cases
5Publish booth placement, cuisine mix, and voucher eligibility before vendors commit.Named directly by Federal Way vendors as the difference between success and failure at the same event
6Require a light, common reporting template as a condition of award.Vendor sales were captured by only 4 of 8 organizers; 4 organizers and 4 businesses asked for tracking tools; Kent and Burien produced no business-level responses at all
7Build a shared equipment and signage pool.8 businesses paid for rentals and 10 for largely single-use décor and branded material
8Convert willing participants into an evidence base now. 14 businesses agreed to interviews or spotlights and 18 want future funding information.Retains the 20 of 28 repeat-intent cohort and supplies the qualitative record the next funding case will need
DATA INTEGRITY NOTES ON THESE SURVEYS

One response reports a range. A SeaTac vendor (Commemorative Sports Towel) reported sales of “$350–$700 per activation.” The $700 upper figure is used in the SeaTac total ($2,950.00) and the program net (−$516.93). At the $350 lower figure, SeaTac nets +$967.28 and the program net is −$866.93. No conclusion on this page changes.

The exported files are each missing one response. The business export contains 27 of 28 recorded responses and the organizer export 7 of 8. In both cases the absent record is a Skyway participant. Cross-referencing the response summaries identifies them as the Skyway Coalition organizer record and the Beachcomber Bar & Grill business record. Counts on this page use the full recorded totals of 28 and 8; the revenue and spending arithmetic uses only the 25 businesses in the export that reported both figures, so the Beachcomber record — free food and merchandise given away against about $1,000 spent — is excluded. Including it would widen the net result to roughly −$1,500.

Revenue and spending were free-text entries, not validated fields. Several were ranges or multi-event totals. Where a range was given the upper bound is used; where a figure covered multiple dates it is counted once. Two businesses could not state revenue and are excluded from the paired arithmetic.

Self-reported, unaudited, and not receipts-verified. These are participant recollections collected after the fact, not point-of-sale records. They should be cited as survey findings and not merged into the receipts-based tax calculation elsewhere in this dashboard.

Kent and Burien have organizer activity but no business-level responses. Kent Chamber reported reaching 54 businesses and Burien appears in the fund’s scope, yet neither produced a single business survey response. Any citywide comparison must state this absence rather than imply a zero result.

THE FUND MEASURED HERE IS A SEPARATE, LATER ROUND FROM THE $250K GAME READY GRANTS
These are frequently conflated. The $250,000 Game Ready Activation Grants were a pre-tournament round funded by King County lodging tax and an interlocal agreement with the Port of Seattle, awarded in four tiers from $2,500 to $20,000, promoted for communities outside Seattle, and required to finish by December 27, 2025. The World Cup Small Business Activation Grant — the Watch Party & Business Activation Fund measured on this page — ran during the tournament in summer 2026 and is a distinct award cycle; the Chamber’s own Playbook describes it as watch-party funding in South King County and unincorporated areas. The Chamber states that round is closed with all funds allocated, but its total dollar value has not been made public, which is why this page reports participant outcomes and cannot compute a program-wide return on investment. Obtaining that total is the single highest-value disclosure for evaluating the Chamber’s investment.
WHAT THE PILOT PROVED BEFORE THE WORLD CUP ROUND
The CBC pilot’s published outcomes give the Chamber a documented track record: 2,000+ small businesses reached across 31 jurisdictions, 700+ referrals, 102 jobs retained and 93 new jobs created, $282,000 in capital investment, nearly $1M in contracts distributed, and $35,000 routed to local partners for collaborative outreach, with 90% of businesses served BIPOC and/or women-owned. The seven pilot Connectors were Lake City Collective, OneEastside Spark, Growing Contigo LLC, the International Rescue Committee, Indian American Community Services, the Kent Chamber of Commerce, and SnoValley Chamber. Notably, Seattle itself was not a designated service area — the model was built for the rest of King County from the outset.
The Chamber’s role in the tournament

Outside Seattle, the Chamber was the tournament’s main small-business channel. It served as SeattleFWC26’s official small-business liaison and as King County’s designated Associate Development Organization, and it runs the CBC network through which every round on this page was delivered.

HOW THE TWO ROUNDS CONNECT

Hubs 3 and 4, highlighted, cover every community in the Watch Party & Business Activation Fund. In the Game Ready round they reported 102 small businesses, about 3,300 participants, 30 expected jobs and 28 retained staff. Hub 4 — Federal Way, Kent and Maple Valley–Black Diamond — had the lowest share of grantees planning a World Cup activation (40%). The Watch Party round then produced both ends of the result: Maple Valley–Black Diamond’s +400% and Federal Way’s −$11,018.

The Game Ready report publishes grantee self-reports of reach and intent, not business revenue or cost. The Watch Party surveys analysed on this page add that layer — individual business revenue against cost — which is the evidence the next funding round needs. One reconciliation point: the report’s headline cites 72 activations across 15 King County cities, while its 15 area snapshots (14 cities plus unincorporated areas) itemise 52; the Chamber can confirm which count is final. THE CENTRAL EQUITY FINDING

Seattle’s arts and culture allocation alone was 9.2 times the CBC Game Ready total that served the rest of King County, and roughly 7.3 times as much per funded organization. Counting the Department of Neighborhoods investment, Seattle-directed activation funding approached $3.6M against $250,000 for the balance of the county — a ratio of about 14 to 1. The single largest watch party in the region, HOMETEAM’s Brick Park site in Pioneer Square, drew nearly 20,000 for USA–Australia on June 19, more than triple the 6,665 combined attendance recorded across all eight fund-supported South King County activations.

Kent Chamber CEO Zenovia Harris named this directly ahead of the tournament: “We are not going to allow all of the money to go to those businesses in Seattle.” The survey results on this page are the measured test of that effort — and they show the smaller South King County activations produced a net −$516.93 across 25 reporting businesses, concentrated almost entirely in one central-festival model, while the host-venue model returned positive results at a fraction of the cost.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE NEXT INVESTMENT CYCLE
The evidence supports a specific reallocation rather than a larger budget. Maple Valley–Black Diamond returned +$7,700.95 on $1,925 of business spending by routing grants directly to existing businesses that hosted their own viewing — a +400% return with no event infrastructure. Federal Way absorbed 82% of all business spending in the program and returned −$11,018.16, because vendors paid booth fees, inventory and staffing against attendance that did not materialize; 18 of 28 businesses named low attendance as their top challenge. The Chamber’s own participants point the same direction: 20 of 28 would repeat, 21 want funding, 20 want marketing support, and 13 want business matchmaking, while 7 of 8 organizers would host again and 17 of 28 businesses cited community connection as the top benefit even where the money did not work. Demand is real; the delivery model is what needs to change.
SCOPE AND PROVENANCE
Findings on this page are drawn from two Microsoft Forms instruments administered after the activations: the 2026 World Cup Watch Party & Business Activation Post-Event Survey for organizers (8 responses, average completion 246 minutes) and the Small Business Participant Survey (28 responses, average completion 26 minutes). Both cover activations supported through the Seattle Metro Chamber’s Community Business Connector World Cup Watch Party & Business Activation Fund, spanning Kent, SeaTac, Burien, Federal Way, White Center, Skyway, and Maple Valley–Black Diamond. Analysis prepared by The Data Guys™ under agreement with the Kent Chamber of Commerce. These are program-participant outcomes and are reported separately from the regional tournament estimates elsewhere in this dashboard; they are not additive to them.

THE DEMAND THAT STAYED AWAY IN JUNE CAME BACK IN AUGUST

Match-week hotel occupancy was 73.9%; once the tournament left it rose to 90.5%. August then became downtown’s busiest visitor month in more than seven years, with hotel rooms sold up 3% on August 2025. The regular summer visitors who avoided the crowds and prices did not disappear — they rescheduled. That is displacement in its plainest form, and it is why this analysis deducts it rather than counting every June dollar as new.

The labour data tells the same story from the other side. Washington added about 10,700 leisure and hospitality jobs from May through July, and state economists called their durability “unclear.” August answered: the sector shed 3,700 statewide, 3,500 of them in accommodation and food services — roughly one in three of the tournament-season gain. The Seattle metro lost about 700 jobs overall; its unemployment rate was a preliminary 4.8%. MyNorthwest / DSA DSA dashboard WA ESD, Aug 2026 BLS Seattle MSA WSDOT

READING THE TRANSIT RECORDS CORRECTLY

Link’s records are real and Class A — 5.4M boardings in June, nearly a million above the previous monthly high, and 309,000 on July 6. But the baseline moved before the tournament began: the Crosslake Connection opened in March and Link ridership jumped 46% in April, making it the busiest light rail system in the country. The fair World Cup attribution is the increment above the post-Crosslake baseline — on the order of the ~1M-boarding margin over the prior record — not the full 5.4M. The system carried the record without a major breakdown, according to Sound Transit’s post-tournament review. Sound Transit APTA Passenger Transport Seattle Transit Blog

1. Economic Impact Reconciliation — $489M modeled FORECAST + MODELED

Status: Visit Seattle released the official post-event result on September 22, 2026 — $889M, prepared by Tourism Economics. The full report and methodology have not been released publicly as of September 29, 2026, so an independent estimate ($489M documented floor) has been triangulated from published receipts and reconciled to the official figure through three disclosed assumptions.

MetricValueSource
Original Visit Seattle projection$929MVisit Seattle (Dec 2024)
Revised forecast$845.6MVisit Seattle (trimmed ~9%)
Independent 5-method triangulation$489M central estimateIndependent modeling
National post-event (NY/NJ)$3.5B (+6% above forecast)NJEDA
National WC hotel revenue forecast~$900M additionalTourism Economics
Global WC gross output (pre-event)~$80B projectedFIFA
Global WC actual (BofA)~$40BBank of America
Visit Seattle projected jobs20,000+Visit Seattle
Visit Seattle projected visitors750,000Visit Seattle

What we have: Pre-event forecast ($929M → $845.6M), independent triangulated estimate ($489M), national benchmark (NY/NJ $3.5B), FIFA global projection ($80B vs BofA actual $40B).

Briefing note: The $489M triangulation uses 5 methods (top-down, bottom-up, BofA implied, DSA implied, tax implied) with displacement adjustment. The gap between $845.6M forecast and $489M is 42%, consistent with the national pattern (FIFA projected $80B, BofA measured $40B — a 50% gap).

  • 4 fan zone attendance totals (Puyallup, Spokane, Tri-Cities, Vancouver WA): Events documented but attendance not published; 5 of 9 have public totals
  • Local procurement dollar total: Program infrastructure documented (Small Business Initiative, 3 liaisons, playbook, WSDOT RFQQ); dollar total not published
  • Per-match transit fare revenue: Sound Transit published Jun 19 data (172K payments); full match-day breakdown not run for every match
  • Seattle-specific media value: Nielsen provides per-match TV audience; Seattle-specific brand value not separately quantified
  • ESD payroll data: Sector employment (10,700 jobs) published; WC-specific payroll dollars not separately reported

Sources & Methodology
150+ cited sources behind the verified core · independent realized-impact methodology · Sources reviewed Sep 29, 2026
Realized-Impact Methodology

1. Geography: Report Seattle, King County and Washington statewide separately

2. Event window: Match days + justified shoulder days; keep broader summer context separate

3. Incremental visitors: Combine ticket origin, Placer/Datafy, airport and lodging; deduplicate repeat visits

4. Direct visitor spend: Use visitor-origin card spend + lodging + transportation + event spend; subtract local substitution

5. Labor/indirect effects: Use transparent multipliers only after direct spend and labor income are reconciled

6. Fiscal return: Use actual DOR/City receipts, not forecasted tax rates alone

7. Displacement: Account for hotel/convention displacement, local avoidance, CID/Pioneer Square differences

8. Public cost: Actual expenditure less reimbursements/grants; disclose capital separately by useful life/legacy

9. Distribution: Report neighborhood, sector, business type, worker and statewide fan-zone outcomes

10. Confidence: Attach evidence class, data owner, extraction date and methodology to every headline metric

CORE FORMULA
Net realized benefit = incremental visitor/event direct spending + attributable labor income/indirect effects + attributable fiscal benefits − displaced normal activity − local substitution/leakage − incremental public operating costs. Capital investments should be disclosed separately with legacy/useful-life treatment.
